name: Same Sum Blocks (Hard)
description: This problem is given in two editions, which differ exclusively in the constraints on the number $$$n$$$. You are given an array of integers $$$a[1], a[2], \dots, a[n].$$$ A block is a sequence of contiguous (consecutive) elements $$$a[l], a[l+1], \dots, a[r]$$$ ($$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$). Thus, a block is defined by a pair of indices $$$(l, r)$$$. Find a set of blocks $$$(l_1, r_1), (l_2, r_2), \dots, (l_k, r_k)$$$ such that: They do not intersect (i.e. they are disjoint). Formally, for each pair of blocks $$$(l_i, r_i)$$$ and $$$(l_j, r_j$$$) where $$$i \neq j$$$ either $$$r_i \lt l_j$$$ or $$$r_j \lt l_i$$$. For each block the sum of its elements is the same. Formally, $$$$$$a[l_1]+a[l_1+1]+\dots+a[r_1]=a[l_2]+a[l_2+1]+\dots+a[r_2]=$$$$$$ $$$$$$\dots =$$$$$$ $$$$$$a[l_k]+a[l_k+1]+\dots+a[r_k].$$$$$$ The number of the blocks in the set is maximum. Formally, there does not exist a set of blocks $$$(l_1', r_1'), (l_2', r_2'), \dots, (l_{k'}', r_{k'}')$$$ satisfying the above two requirements with $$$k' \gt k$$$. The picture corresponds to the first example. Blue boxes illustrate blocks. Write a program to find such a set of blocks.
input_specification: The first line contains integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 1500$$$) — the length of the given array. The second line contains the sequence of elements $$$a[1], a[2], \dots, a[n]$$$ ($$$-10^5 \le a_i \le 10^5$$$).
output_specification: In the first line print the integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n$$$). The following $$$k$$$ lines should contain blocks, one per line. In each line print a pair of indices $$$l_i, r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n$$$) — the bounds of the $$$i$$$-th block. You can print blocks in any order. If there are multiple answers, print any of them.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1141F2 — Same Sum Blocks (Hard) [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
